paper_title: On the Limits of Scale: Inverse Scaling in Vision-Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Scaling laws suggest that increasing model size, training data, and compute generally yields monotonic performance improvements. While this often holds at the aggregate level, we present systematic evidence that vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit inverse scaling at the subtask level: specific question categories on which larger models perform worse than smaller counterparts within the same model family. We evaluate 19 models from four distinct model families across eight multimodal benchmarks (nine evaluation splits), answering 29,386 questions per model, 558,334 model-question evaluations in total. Using per-question pairwise analysis across all model pairs in each family, we identify 375 subtask-model-pair combinations exhibiting inverse scaling, spanning 4,342 unique queries where a smaller model answers correctly but a larger model fails, and we find that these patterns replicate across independently developed architectures. We identify 13 subtask-dataset pairs that show inverse scaling across multiple families, consistent with the phenomenon being task-driven rather than model-specific. The most affected domains in our study include multi-image spatial reasoning, visual perception, and university-level STEM knowledge, with accuracy gaps exceeding 20 percentage points in several cases, while diagram understanding appears comparatively resistant. These findings challenge the assumption that increasing model size uniformly improves multimodal capabilities and suggest that model selection should be task-aware.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Neural scaling laws suggest that model performance generally improves with increasing model size, data, and compute (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022). This empirical trend has guided the development of foundation models and reinforced simple working assumption: larger models should perform better. However, recent work shows that this assumption can fail. In language models, McKenzie et al. (2023) identify inverse scaling tasks on which performance worsens as model scale increases, while Wei et al. (2023) show that some of these trends are better described as non-monotonic or U-shaped behaviour rather than uniformly decreasing. More recently, Gema et al. (2025) demonstrate an analogous phenomenon for reasoning models, where increasing test-time compute can also reduce accuracy. In multimodal reasoning, concurrent work by Bae et al. (2025) shows that adding visual distractors can reduce VLMs accuracy and induce inverse-scaling-like behaviour, though in constructed distractor setting rather than in standard benchmark evaluation. Whether inverse scaling also arises in VLMs under standard benchmark evaluation, without artificially introducing distractors, remains an open question. VLMs inherit the same scaling paradigm as language models, with model families typically released in sizes ranging from small to very large. At the same time, VLMs must jointly process visual and textual information, creating additional opportunities for failure (Asadi et al., 2026; Saxena et al., 2026). larger model may achieve higher overall benchmark accuracy while becoming less accurate on particular forms of visual reasoning. If so, standard aggregate evaluation may obscure regressions that are scientifically important and 1Our code is available at https://github.com/saxenarohit/vlm inverse scaling 1 Figure 1: Scaling curves for four cross-family subtasks. Filled circles: dense models; open diamonds: MoE variants. All show non-monotonic behaviour across families. practically relevant for deployment. Such regressions are already visible, though unremarked, in providers own reports: in the Qwen3-VL technical report (Bai et al., 2025), the 8B instruct model scores above both the 32B and the 30B-A3B on BLINK (69.1 vs. 67.3 and 67.7; Tables 34), the 32B scores above the 235B-A22B on VLMs-Are-Blind (87.0 vs. 80.4; Tables 23), and CountBench accuracy declines monotonically from 2B to 4B to 8B (88.4, 84.9, 80.5; Table 4). Aggregate reporting records these numbers without identifying which capabilities regress or on which questions. In this work, we conduct systematic study of subtask-level inverse scaling across model sizes in vision-language models on standard multimodal benchmarks, where subtasks are the category labels provided by each benchmark (e.g., Jigsaw in BLINK (Fu et al., 2024) or Organic Chemistry in MMMU (Yue et al., 2023); see Table 1 for the full list of benchmarks). Our analysis is structured around within-family comparisons: we compare models released under the same family name, which generally share high-level architecture and training recipe but may differ across sizes in language backbone, vision encoder, active parameter count, training data, alignment procedure, or inferencetime visual processing. This design reduces, but does not eliminate, confounds relative to comparisons across independently developed model families. We evaluate 19 models from four distinct model families (Qwen3-VL (Bai et al., 2025), InternVL3.5 (Wang et al., 2025), Gemma 3 (Team et al., 2025), and Molmo 2 (Clark et al., 2026)) spanning roughly 1B to 235B total parameters and including both dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) variants. Across eight established multimodal benchmarks used for evaluating frontier VLMs (nine evaluation splits), this yields 29,386 questions per model. Rather than relying solely on aggregate accuracy, we introduce per-question flip analysis that compares the behaviour of paired models on the same evaluation items, measuring how often smaller model answers correctly when larger model fails, and vice versa. This paired analysis quantifies inverse scaling at the subtask level, revealing patterns that are often hidden in benchmark-level summaries. Our results show that inverse scaling is widespread at the subtask level (Figure 1). Across all pairwise comparisons within each family, we identify 375 subtaskmodel-pair cases exhibiting inverse scaling, spanning all four model families and appearing in every benchmark we evaluate. These patterns are not confined to single architecture or training recipe: 13 subtaskdataset pairs exhibit inverse scaling across multiple families (Figure 2), consistent with task-driven rather than purely model-specific phenomenon. The strongest effects arise in multi-image spatial reasoning (BLINK), multi-task visual understanding (MMT-Bench), and university-level STEM problem solving (MMMU), whereas diagram understanding (AI2D) appears comparatively resistant. Crucially, these findings persist when restricting to dense-only model pairs (193 cases, 8 cross-family subtasks), confirming that the phenomenon is not driven solely by MoE models. Appendix presents qualitative examples illustrating the range of failure modes, from misidentifying clearly visible objects to selecting plausible but incorrect options. These findings challenge the assumption that increasing scale uniformly improves multimodal capability. More broadly, they suggest that model choice should depend not only on aggregate benchmark performance, but also on the specific capabilities required by the target application domain (Liu et al., 2025).

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Scaling laws. Scaling-law work shows that language-model loss and many downstream capabilities improve predictably as parameters, data, and compute increase (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022). Similar empirical regularities have also been reported in vision-language pretraining: Cherti et al. (2023) find power-law behaviour for CLIP-style contrastive models across zero-shot classification, retrieval, linear probing, and fine-tuning. Similarly, Aghajanyan et al. (2023) reports relevant scaling laws for multimodal models. While these works focus on aggregate task performance, we analyse whether monotonic improvements persist at the finer-grained level of benchmark subtasks within VLM family, which we assume correlates more directly with specific multimodal skills. Inverse scaling in LLMs and VLMs. The Inverse Scaling Prize (McKenzie et al., 2023) introduced curated text-only tasks on which larger language models performed worse and identified causes such as strong priors, unwanted imitation, and distractor tasks. Wei et al. (2023) expanded the model range and found that many of these curves become U-shaped rather than monotonically decreasing, and that one-shot examples or chain-of-thought prompting can mitigate some failures. Along different axis, Gema et al. (2025) construct tasks on which extending the reasoning length of large reasoning models degrades accuracy, yielding inverse scaling in test-time compute rather than model size. Concurrently, Bae et al. (2025) study how visual and textual distractors affect multimodal reasoning, finding that visual distractors reduce VLM accuracy without lengthening reasoning chains, mechanism distinct from text-only distractor effects. Our work complements these efforts by examining open VLM families on standard multimodal benchmarks rather than on specially constructed tasks and by detecting inverse scaling via perquestion pairwise flips within existing subtasks. In line with McKenzie et al. (2023), our findings are observational evidence from publicly available VLM checkpoints.

sections.title: 4.1 EVALUATION PROTOCOL
sections.content: Inference. All models are evaluated zero-shot with direct prompting and greedy decoding, with thinking modes disabled to separate model scale from test-time compute (Gema et al., 2025); MCQ prompts ask for the option letter and open-ended prompts for concise answer (settings in Appendix A, prompts in Appendix G). Answers are verified as in VLMEvalKit (Duan et al., 2025): deterministic letter extraction and exact or numeric matching, with GPT-5.4 as multimodal fallback adjudicator when these rules are inconclusive (0.4% of responses). Case selection. We report pairwise inverse-scaling case when the subtask contains at least 20 shared questions and the net flip advantage is Net 5. The first threshold excludes subtasks too small for meaningful comparison; the second excludes cases where the asymmetry is trivially small. The findings are robust to stricter thresholds: 132 cases across 44 subtaskdataset pairs remain at Net 10, with 4 cross-family subtasks still replicated (Appendix F).

sections.title: 5.5 OTHER FINDINGS
sections.content: MoE models frequently appear in inverse scaling pairs. Mixture-of-Experts models frequently appear as the larger model in inverse scaling pairs. Qwen 30B-A3B (3B active parameters) underperforms the dense 32B model on several BLINK subtasks. InternVL 241B-A28B (28B active) fails to improve over the dense 38B on AI2D (both 87.1%) and degrades on several BLINK subtasks. However, MoE and dense models differ in active parameter count, training recipe, and alignment procedure, so we cannot isolate the contribution of expert routing from these confounds. The findings above show that inverse scaling is widespread and cross-family, but is it simply the largest model underperforming, or more complex relationship between scale and capability? Three observations suggest the latter. Scaling trajectories are non-monotonic. Rather than single large-model drop, many subtasks exhibit multiple peaks and valleys across the size range. For example, InternVLs performance on Mechanics of Materials on MMMU shows: 1B = 27.6%, 2B = 48.3%, 4B = 44.8%, 8B = 31.0%, 14B = 51.7%, 30B-A3B = 58.6%, 38B = 62.1%, 241B-A28B = 27.6%. This suggests that different model sizes have qualitatively different strengths rather than uniformly improving capabilities. In extreme cases, the smallest model wins. This non-monotonicity can be so pronounced that the smallest model in family achieves the highest subtask accuracy. Qwen 2B is the best on MMMU test AI Content Detection (65.0% vs. 235Bs 45.0%). sections.title: 5.6 ERROR TAXONOMY
sections.content: To understand why larger models fail on inverse-scaling questions, we use GPT-5.4 as multimodal annotator to assign failure categories to inverse-scaling flip examples. We sample up to 10 flip questions per pairwise case with stratified dataset quotas and per-family cap of 600, yielding 1,300 questions spanning eight datasets and all 4 families after filtering degenerate responses (empty or single non-letter characters). Each question, along with its associated image(s), is independently classified (temperature = 0) into one of three failure categories. The annotator prompt is blinded to model identities (models are labeled Model and Model B) to reduce bias. As secondary check, we also run Claude Opus 4.6 with the same prompt; the two judges agree on 90.8% of questions (Cohens κ = 0.30). Full prompts and API model identifiers are provided in Appendix G. To validate the LLM annotations, three authors independently labeled stratified subsample of 127 questions using the same three categories. Human inter-annotator agreement was substantial (Fleiss κ = 0.65, pairwise agreement 8792%). The human majority vote classified 84.3% as genuine errors and 15.7% as bad annotation or ambiguous, confirming that humans identify more annotation issues than either LLM judge (GPT: 2.6%, Claude: 10.5%). The majority vote agreed with GPT on 88.2% and with Claude on 84.3% of questions (full breakdown in Appendix H). Of the 1,300 sampled flips, GPT-5.4 classified 97.4% (1,266) as genuine errors, 2.6% (34) as bad annotation or ambiguous, and none as format mismatch. All five raters (three human, two LLM) classify the majority as genuine errors, though with different thresholds: GPT-5.4 labels 97.4% as genuine, while the human majority vote applies stricter standard, classifying 84.3% as genuine and flagging 15.7% as bad annotation or ambiguous. We use the human rate as our conservative estimate: at least 84% of inverse scaling flips reflect real model failures. The human-flagged bad-annotation cases are concentrated in MME (known annotation issues) and knowledge-heavy benchmarks where 8 ground-truth answers are debatable; on visual reasoning benchmarks (BLINK, ScienceQA), both humans and LLMs agree that nearly all flips are genuine errors.

sections.title: 6 DISCUSSION
sections.content: Why does inverse scaling occur in VLMs? While our study does not establish causal explanations, several hypotheses fit the observed patterns. First, localized capability regression: on some perceptioncentric subtasks (BLINK, MME), larger released variants are less accurate than smaller ones, even though the larger model is ahead in 74.8% of eligible comparisons. These regressions affect particular skills, not whole benchmarks, and our data cannot attribute them to parameter count alone. Second, sensitivity to distractors: on knowledge-heavy benchmarks (MMMU, MMT-Bench), larger models may be more susceptible to plausible but incorrect options, consistent with the distractor memorization hypothesis of McKenzie et al. (2023). Third, MoE-specific factors: MoE variants frequently appear in inverse scaling pairs, though routing, lower active parameter counts, and training differences cannot be separated in our observational data. Fourth, training data composition: larger models typically see more training data, whose composition may introduce biases that hurt specific subtasks. Can chain-of-thought prompting recover the errors? To test whether inverse scaling errors reflect shallow reasoning deficits, we re-evaluated both models of every case under chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting on all shared questions (66,698 matched question instances across 375 cases). The CoT prompt adds step-by-step instruction to the direct prompt (Appendix L); decoding is unchanged. CoT attenuates inverse scaling but does not remove it: the median Net falls from +8 to 0, yet 96 of 375 cases (25.6%) retain Net 5, 101 reverse, and the larger model recovers 43.5% of the questions it had lost under direct prompting. Persistence varies by benchmark, from 48.6% of MME and 42.1% of BLINK cases to 7.6% on MMMU test (full results in Appendix L). Because the smaller model is also re-evaluated, the persisting cases cannot be attributed to the smaller model reasoning where the larger one does not. CoT thus corrects fewer than half of the individual errors and leaves quarter of the cases intact, and part of the reduction in Net comes from the smaller model losing accuracy under CoT (in 251 of 375 cases) rather than from the larger model gaining. It also remains an open question whether CoT recovery reflects genuine improvements in reasoning, as recent work suggests that intermediate steps can sometimes mask underlying vulnerabilities (Xu et al., 2025; Kambhampati et al., 2025; Shojaee et al., 2025). Implications for model selection. Our results have practical implications. The common practice of selecting the largest available model is suboptimal for some task categories. On minority of evaluated subtaskmodel-pair comparisons, concentrated in multi-image spatial reasoning, visual perception, and specific STEM subtasks, smaller models outperform their larger counterparts. Practitioners should evaluate candidate models on their downstream tasks, not on aggregate scores. Limitations. Our study has several limitations. First, we evaluate only open-weight models, since the unknown architectures and parameter counts of proprietary models make scaling analysis unverifiable. Second, the flip analysis weights all questions equally, regardless of difficulty. Third, cross-family replication reports empirical evidence and does not establish any causal mechanism. Fourth, models released under one family name may differ in vision encoder (Appendix K), training data, alignment, and active parameters, so our results describe subtask-level regressions among released variants rather than causal effects of parameter count alone; controlled study training VLMs of several sizes under one fully released recipe would isolate parameter count and make such analyses reproducible, which we leave to future work. Fifth, larger checkpoints may have seen more benchmark data, and we cannot rule out size-dependent contamination. Sixth, results depend on option order; the strongest BLINK cases survive reorderings (Appendix J), but paraphrases are untested.

sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: To our knowledge, this is the first systematic study of inverse scaling in vision-language models. We evaluate 19 models across 4 families and eight benchmarks. Through per-question pairwise analysis, we identify 375 cases in which smaller models outperform larger ones, with 13 subtask types showing this pattern across multiple families. Our findings demonstrate that VLM performance does not scale monotonically at the subtask level, with multi-image spatial reasoning, visual perception, and specialized STEM knowledge most affected. These results motivate work on the mechanisms of 9 inverse scaling and suggest task-aware model deployment. Finally, this work complements recent evidence of deficiencies in current VLMs (e.g., Asadi et al. (2026)), highlighting the need for robust multimodal models that leverage their full capacity across modalities.

sections.title: D STATISTICAL SIGNIFICANCE ANALYSIS
sections.content: We report one-sided McNemar exact p-values as descriptive measure of paired asymmetry for each of the 375 candidate cases; case is one subtaskmodel-pair comparison (a subtask, smaller model, and larger model of the same family), and each test is computed over that subtasks shared questions. For each case, we construct 2 2 contingency table of per-question outcomes between the smaller and larger model. Under the null hypothesis that both models are equally likely to answer correctly, the number of discordant-inverse outcomes (FlipInv) follows Binomial(FlipInv + FlipNorm, 0.5) distribution. These p-values are exploratory, not confirmatory, for two reasons: (1) cases were pre-selected using the same observed data (Net 5, 20), which biases the tested set toward positive effects; and (2) the tests involve many overlapping model-pair/subtask combinations. They should be read as descriptive characterization of effect strength, not as family-wise error-controlled evidence. To address (2), we also report BenjaminiHochberg (BH) adjusted p-values (FDR 0.05), corrected either over the 375 cases or, more conservatively, over the full space of 10,434 eligible within-family comparisons (n 20) from which the cases were selected. 24 Table 35: McNemars exact test significance by Net range, uncorrected and after BenjaminiHochberg (BH) correction at FDR 0.05. sections.title: G EVALUATION PROMPTS
sections.content: All models receive identical prompts per dataset. We use direct (zero-shot, no chain-of-thought) prompting throughout to isolate model capacity from reasoning scaffolding. Multiple-choice datasets. For MCQ datasets (MMT-Bench, MMMU, ScienceQA, MMBench), the prompt is constructed as: [Question] A. [Option A] B. [Option B] C. [Option C] ... Please select the correct answer from the options above. Respond with only the letter of the correct option. explain. Answer: Do not MMBench additionally prepends hint field (image context description) before the question when available. MMMU questions may contain embedded <image N> placeholders referencing multiple sub-images within the question text. Open-ended questions. MMMU contains subset of fill-in-the-blank questions without multiplechoice options. For these, the suffix is replaced with: Answer concisely with just the final value or term. Answer: Yes/No dataset (MME). MME questions are presented as-is without any additional suffix. Each question expects Yes or No response. Pre-formatted datasets. AI2D, MathVista, and BLINK use pre-formatted prompts from their respective source distributions. AI2D uses the VLMEvalKit-processed version with masked diagrams. MathVista uses the query field from AI4Math/MathVista, which includes task-specific hints and answer format instructions. BLINK prompts are used verbatim from the original benchmark. G.1 ERROR TAXONOMY JUDGE For the error analysis (Section 5.6), we classify each inverse scaling flip question using GPT5.4 and Claude Opus 4.6 as multimodal annotators. GPT-5.4 is accessed via the OpenAI API (model identifier: gpt-5.4). Claude Opus 4.6 is accessed via the Anthropic API (model identifier: claude-opus-4-6). Each question is sent with its associated image(s) and the following text prompt (temperature = 0, max tokens = 200). The prompt is blinded to model identities; models are labeled Model (correct) and Model (incorrect) without revealing their sizes: You are analyzing VLM (Vision-Language Model) benchmark results. Two models answered this question. Model answered correctly and Model answered incorrectly. Your job is to figure out why Model failed. Question: {question} Options: {options} Correct Answer: {answer} Model response: {response_small} -> CORRECT Model response: {response_large} -> INCORRECT Categorize Model Bs failure into exactly ONE of these categories: 1. GENUINE_ERROR - Model made clear mistake -- whether through visual misidentification, wrong reasoning, incorrect knowledge, falling for plausible distractor, or simply picking the wrong answer. This covers any case where the model genuinely got it wrong. 2. FORMAT_MISMATCH - Model effectively gives the correct answer content, but in form that would not match the benchmark answer format (e.g., numeric value instead of option letter, or full option text instead of just the letter). If the response is self-contradictory or clearly commits to the wrong answer, use GENUINE_ERROR. 3. BAD_ANNOTATION_OR_AMBIGUOUS - Use this only when there is strong evidence that the ground-truth answer is wrong, the question is genuinely ambiguous, or multiple answers would reasonably be acceptable. Do NOT use this category just 27 because Model Bs answer seems plausible; if the benchmark answer is still clearly better supported, use GENUINE_ERROR. Reply with ONLY JSON object (no markdown, no extra text): {"category": "CATEGORY_NAME", "confidence": "high/medium/low", "explanation": "One concise sentence explaining why."} Each annotator assigns exactly one category per question. We report GPT-5.4 results in the main text and use Claude Opus 4.6 as secondary check. The two judges agree on 90.8% of questions (Cohens κ = 0.30; Section 5.6). We treat these annotations as exploratory qualitative labels, not as validated ground truth.

sections.title: K VISION ENCODERS AND IMAGE PREPROCESSING
sections.content: Within-family comparisons hold the training recipe roughly fixed but not necessarily the vision encoder. Table 44 lists, for each model, the vision encoder as stated in the familys technical report or model card and confirmed against the released configuration files. Two families change encoder across sizes: Qwen3-VL uses SigLIP2-Large (300M) for the 2B and 4B models and SigLIP2-SO400M for the larger ones (Bai et al., 2025), and InternVL3.5 uses InternViT-300M up to the 14B model and 30B-A3B and InternViT-6B for the 38B and 241B-A28B (Wang et al., 2025); in both, the encoder is trained jointly, so same-tier weights may still differ across sizes. Gemma 3 shares one frozen 417M SigLIP encoder across all three sizes (Team et al., 2025), and Molmo 2 uses the same SigLIP 2 SO-400M configuration for both sizes (Clark et al., 2026). All models use their native dynamic-resolution or tiling preprocessing at the defaults of their released processors, with no image resizing on our side. Of the 375 cases, 271 (72.3%) compare two models with the same encoder tier (Qwen3-VL 68, InternVL3.5 157, Gemma 3 26, Molmo 2 20); the 46 Gemma 3 and Molmo 2 cases compare models whose encoders are shared or configuration-identical, so only the language model differs in size. The remaining 104 cases cross an encoder tier (Qwen3-VL 54, InternVL3.5 50), and in every InternVL3.5 instance the larger model is the one with the roughly twenty times larger encoder. Restricting the cross-family analysis to same-tier cases leaves 10 of the 13 replicated subtasks, including BLINK Multi-view Reasoning in all four families. 30 Table 44: Vision encoders by model. We re-evaluate both models of every case under CoT prompting on all shared questions of the subtask: 375 cases, 66,698 matched question instances, and 92,694 modelquestion evaluations over 522 (model, dataset, subtask) runs. The CoT prompt appends step-by-step instruction to the dataset prompt; for multiple-choice questions it reads: Answer the preceding multiple choice question. The last line of your response should be of the following format: Answer: $LETTER (without quotes) where LETTER is one of options. Think step by step before answering. Decoding is greedy with 4,096-token budget, and answers are scored with the same pipeline as the direct condition. Because both models are re-run, Net is recomputed from the CoT outputs rather than adjusted. Result. Table 45 reports the outcome per family and Table 46 per dataset. CoT attenuates inverse scaling but does not remove it. The median Net falls from +8 to 0; 96 of 375 cases (25.6%) retain Net 5, 178 fall below the threshold, and 101 reverse sign (Net 5). The larger model recovers 3,640 of the 8,361 questions (43.5%) it had lost under direct prompting. At the same time, the smaller models accuracy decreases under CoT in 251 of 375 cases (mean 3.9pp, vs. +5.2pp for the larger model), so part of the reduction in Net reflects the smaller model losing its advantage rather than the larger model gaining. Where it persists. Persistence differs markedly across benchmarks. On MME and BLINK, close to half of the cases survive CoT (48.6% and 42.1%), whereas on MMMU the effect largely disappears: 7.6% of test-split cases persist and 41 of 105 reverse. One reading is that CoT helps more where the difficulty lies in reasoning over recognized content than where it lies in extracting the answer from the image, but we have not tested this directly. Significance. Applying the test of Appendix to the CoT outcomes, 44 of the 96 persisting cases have uncorrected < 0.05, and 18 remain significant after BH correction over the 375 CoT tests (14 with Net 21), vs. 54 of the same cases under direct prompting.
